abstract: We prove the existence of two thresholds regarding the compilability of random 2-CNF formulas to OBDDs. The formulas are drawn from F₂(n,δn), the uniform distribution over all 2-CNFs with δ n clauses and n variables, with δ ≥ 0 a constant. We show that, with high probability, the random 2-CNF admits OBDDs of size polynomial in n if 0 ≤ δ < 1/2 or if δ > 1. On the other hand, for 1/2 < δ < 1, with high probability, the random 2-CNF admits only OBDDs of size exponential in n. It is no coincidence that the two "compilability thresholds" are δ = 1/2 and δ = 1. Both are known thresholds for other CNF properties, namely, δ = 1 is the satisfiability threshold for 2-CNF while δ = 1/2 is the treewidth threshold, i.e., the point where the treewidth of the primal graph jumps from constant to linear in n with high probability.

      Abstract
We prove the existence of two thresholds regarding the compilability of random 2-CNF formulas to
OBDDs. The formulas are drawn from F2 (n, δn), the uniform distribution over all 2-CNFs with δn
clauses and n variables, with δ ≥ 0 a constant. We show that, with high probability, the random
2-CNF admits OBDDs of size polynomial in n if 0 ≤ δ < 1/2 or if δ > 1. On the other hand, for
1/2 < δ < 1, with high probability, the random 2-CNF admits only OBDDs of size exponential in n.
It is no coincidence that the two “compilability thresholds” are δ = 1/2 and δ = 1. Both are known
thresholds for other CNF properties, namely, δ = 1 is the satisfiability threshold for 2-CNF while
δ = 1/2 is the treewidth threshold, i.e., the point where the treewidth of the primal graph jumps
from constant to linear in n with high probability.

 1      Introduction

BDDs (Binary Decision Diagrams) are a very well-known model for representing Boolean
functions. This model is quite natural and has various properties that make it attractive
and therefore has been considerably studied for decades. Here we focus on ordered BDDs, or
OBDDs, which form an important fragment of BDDs thanks to many desirable properties for
practice (canonicity, fast apply, etc.). Because of their practical appeal, research on the limits
of OBDD developed fast, centered around the following question: which functions admit
a small OBDD representation? We will talk of OBDD-size, i.e., the size of a minimal-size
OBDD for the function. In knowledge compilation terms, we want to know which functions
are (potentially) easy to compile into the OBDD language [11], in the sense that they admit
small representations in this language. Unfortunately, many families of functions have
exponential OBDD-size in the number n of variables [31, 5, 29, 19, 9]. Through combinatorial
arguments similar to those already used by Shannon for switching circuits [27], one can even
show that, as n increases, almost all Boolean functions have exponential OBDD-size [30,
Theorem 2.2.2.]. But not all functions are encountered in the wild and we want to focus
on the OBDD-size of simple functions, in particular functions that can be represented with

       Contributions. We focus on random 2-CNFs drawn from F2 (n, m), that is, formulas are
       taken uniformly at random from the set of 2-CNFs that have m clauses over variables
       x1 , . . . , xn . Our 2-CNFs are sparse: we fix a constant δ > 0 and consider the OBDD-size of
       formulas drawn from F2 (n, δn) as n increases. We show the existence of two compilability
       thresholds: δ = 1/2 and δ = 1. While δ < 1/2, the random CNF almost always has polynomial
       OBDD size. If δ > 1, again the OBDD-size is almost always small (constant actually). On
       the other hand, for δ between 1/2 and 1, almost all random 2-CNF have exponential size.
       This paper proves Theorem 1. The proofs of intermediate lemmas and corollaries marked
       with (⋆) appear in the full version of this work.

       Related work. Our work builds on a rich body of results on random 2-CNF formulas. The
       satisfiability threshold (Theorem 2) was established independently by Chvátal and Reed [10]
       and Goerdt [17]. The precise number of satisfying assignments of random 2-SAT formulas
       was determined by Achlioptas et al. [2]. The treewidth threshold we rely on is due to Lee,
       Lee, and Oum [23]. On the knowledge compilation side, phase transitions for compilation
       have been studied experimentally [18]. However, surprisingly, a theoretical investigation is
       still lacking and we have to turn to research on OBDD-based proof systems to find some
       work that considers OBDDs for random CNF, though not in a setting relevant for us [15].
       Our paper provides the first theoretical account of the phase transition behavior in OBDD
       compilation, establishing exact thresholds for random 2-CNF.

2.2      Random Graphs and Graph Parameters
The primal graph of CNF F is the graph whose vertices are the variables of F and where
two variables are connected by an edge if and only if they appear together in a clause, i.e.,
the edge set is {{x, y} | ∃ clause C ∈ F, x ∈ var(C) and y ∈ var(C) and x =      ̸ y}. Note that
it is not a multigraph and that, for 2-CNF, each edge can correspond to at most 4 clauses.
     Treewidth and pathwidth are well-known graph parameters [7, 26]. Their definition
is not necessary for this paper. We simply recall that the treewidth of a graph G is an
integer between 0 and |V (G)| − 1 denoted by tw(G), that measures how close G is to
a forest. Similarly, the pathwidth of G is an integer between 0 and |V (G)| − 1 denoted
by pw(G), that measures how close G is to a disjoint union of paths. It is known that
tw(G) ≤ pw(G) ≤ O(tw(G) log |V (G)|) [7, Corollary 24]. We call primal treewidth and
primal pathwidth of F the treewidth and pathwidth of its primal graph. For convenience,
given a random CNF F drawn from F2 (n, m), we denote by GF the primal graph of F where
the missing variables, i.e., those in Xn \ var(F ), are added as isolated vertices. Adding
isolated vertices to a non-empty graph does not modify its treewidth nor its pathwidth.

        3      Compilability Thresholds
       The property of a 2-CNF we are interested in is its OBDD-size, that is, the size of the
       smallest OBDD that computes it.
           Binary decision diagrams (BDD) are well-known decision diagram representations of
       Boolean functions. A BDD is a directed acyclic graph with a single source and one or two
       sinks labeled 0 and 1. Each internal node is labeled with a Boolean variable and has exactly
       two outgoing edges called 0-edge and 1-edge. The set of variables labeling nodes of a BDD B
       is denoted var(B). A BDD is ordered (OBDD) when, on every source-to-sink path, each
       variable appears at most once and always in the same order. This total order is called the
       variable order of the OBDD. In a BDD B, every complete assignment α to the variables
       corresponds to a single path: we start from the source and follow the α(x)-edge for every
       node labeled with a variable x that is reached; the label of the sink reached is the value
       B(α) computed by B on α. Note that B(α) is also defined for α an assignment to any
       superset X of var(B). Let f be a Boolean function over X. Then we say B computes f
       when B(α) = f (α) for every α ∈ {0, 1}X .

       3.2      Compilability Thresholds for 2-CNF
       Our main result is the proof that, in the case of general 2-CNF formulas drawn F2 (n, δn),
       there are two compilability thresholds, namely δ = 1/2 and δ = 1. Figure 2 provides
       a visual summary of this phenomenon. It is no coincidence that these are exactly the
       satisfiability threshold and the primal treewidth threshold. We restate Theorem 1 for the
       reader’s convenience.

       ▶ Theorem 1 (Compilability Thresholds of 2-CNF to OBDD). Let δ ≥ 0, n ∈ N and F be a
       random formula following F2 (n, δn). There are constants c, d > 0 such that,
          (I) if δ < 1/2, then limn→∞ Pr[OBDD-size(F ) ≤ nc ] = 1
         (II) if 1/2 < δ < 1, then limn→∞ Pr[OBDD-size(F ) ≥ exp(nd )] = 1
        (III) if δ > 1, then limn→∞ Pr[OBDD-size(F ) = 1] = 1

           In the rest of the paper, we dive into the proof of Theorem 1 (II). Before that, we provide
       some intuition behind the proof. We start from an arbitrary minimal-size OBDD B(F )
       for F . This OBDD uses a certain variable order xπ(1) , . . . , xπ(n) . If we split the variable
       order somewhere, say at position k, we get a bipartition of the variables: xπ(1) , . . . , xπ(k) and
       xπ(k+1) , . . . , xπ(n) . Variables are vertices of GF , so we have a bipartition of GF ’s vertices.
       When F has high primal treewidth (which happens almost always), it turns out that there
       is always a position k such that cutting the variable order at k yields a bipartition of GF
       such that there is a large matching between the two parts, i.e., many edges of GF cross from
       xπ(1) , . . . , xπ(k) to xπ(k+1) , . . . , xπ(n) without sharing a vertex (Section 5). Each edge in GF
       corresponds to at least one clause of F , so this large matching corresponds to a subformula
       M (F ) of F that has many solutions. We can show that if exponentially many solutions
       to M (F ) have an extension that satisfies F , then the kth layer of B(F ) has exponentially
       many nodes (Section 6). B(F ) is a minimal-size OBDD for F , so all OBDDs for F have
       exponentially many nodes.

    One last comment about the proof. A careful reader could object that, in terms of graph
parameters, Theorem 9 requires the treewidth to be large and the degree to be small, while
we never discuss the degree for Theorem 1, which may seem odd. And indeed, the fact that
the maximum degree of GF is generally small (less than log(n)) with high probability is
likely important for Theorem 1, but, in a sense, it is already baked into Theorem 26, which
is why we never explicitly need it. Theorem 26 works in the sparse CNF regime only (i.e.,
F2 (n, δn) with δ > 0), which, in itself, forces small degree with high probability.

 8        Discussion and Future Work
Several natural variations of Theorem 1 need to be investigated. First, we can modify the
initial language; for instance, instead of sparse 2-CNF one may consider k-CNF for k > 2, or
even k-XORSAT or k-NAESAT formulas, sparse or dense. Second, the target language can

        also be altered. One direction is to constrain it more, for instance, by saying that the variable
        order of the OBDD is fixed in advance. In that case, we conjecture that the OBDD-size
        is large even below the treewidth threshold, as there is no way to exploit the structure of
        the primal graph through the variable order. In the opposite direction, there are many
        compilation languages that generalize and are more succinct than OBDD [11], which could
        be considered as alternative target languages. We plan to show that Theorem 1 also holds
        for compilation to structured DNNF circuits, and we have, in a sense, paved the way for the
        proof by insisting on working with treewidth rather than pathwidth. We also believe that
        replacing sparse 2-CNF with sparse 3-CNF is feasible. Currently, the exact location of the
        satisfiability threshold for random 3-CNF is unknown. In addition, to our knowledge, the
        satisfiability threshold is not the same as the treewidth threshold (which we are confident
        exists), but the result can perhaps be stated and proved using placeholder symbols instead
        of the actual values.
             We also want to research alternative proofs of Theorem 1. There could be a clever proof
        relying on the fact that, as n increases, almost all 2-CNF formulas represent unate functions,
        i.e., functions that are monotone modulo consistent literal renaming [3]. Note that this is not
        the same as saying that almost all 2-CNF are monotone modulo consistent literal renaming.
        Nevertheless, knowing Theorem 9 for monotone CNFs, there is some hope for a proof of
        Theorem 1 that would try to reduce the CNF to one that is monotone. But this requires
        showing that almost all 2-CNF formulas from F2 (n, δn), for any fixed δ, represent unate
        functions as n increases. This does not derive directly from [3], but sounds plausible.
             Lastly, as a follow-up to [18], empirical evaluations would be insightful. Setting up these
        experiments is not exactly easy since finding the variable order that gives the smallest OBDD
        is NP-hard [8], but that would allow us to see whether phase transitions are actually visible
        for reasonable n at the thresholds given in this paper.
